doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Goodman's absent-mindedness with names and Ziggy Elman
summary: Goodman lived for the clarinet and couldn't remember names; stories from Sid Weiss, Harry James and Ziggy Elman, and a reunion tour with Joe Glaser.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: That’s a good one. He was pretty, I guess, just totally centered on the music. Was that what he was about?

Yeah he was really — you know if he checked into a hotel, if he was on 37, 40, you went to 22 whatever on the other side. Because he’d practice all day. He lived the clarinet, he really did. He was so foggy, really. The only time he ever knew what he was doing was when he played the clarinet. He couldn’t remember names.
How did he hold a band together? Was that someone else’s job really?

Well he chose the musicians he wanted. He had a manager of course, you know that man. I’ll tell you how foggy — now Sid Weiss, the bass player that worked with Benny Goodman on the old band, an old timer, he told me that in the old days, of course I really, Benny liked me and I had a bad temper in those days and I almost hit him actually. And I used to tell him — I can’t use that f word. But you foggy idiot. You know, a foggy idiot. Because he would do some of the dumbest things. And I was just a kid. You know I didn’t know any — and Sid Weiss said nobody in life ever talked to him, because he didn’t know anybody. One time they were going to do a tour with Benny Goodman and they were trying to get all the original guys that were still alive and — this is a true story — and Louis Armstrong’s band. Before I tell you this, when I worked with him I once asked him — I said I wanted to be around him all day. I was so in awe of him. I said, “Benny, who was your favorite lead trumpet player?” And I’m following him around like a little kid, pulling the string. He said, “Bunny Berigan and Doug Mettome.” I said, “What did you think of Harry James?” He says, “I didn’t know him.” And he walks away from me. I said wait a minute. “Harry James.” “I didn’t know him.” Now that’s what Sid Weiss told me, that he didn’t know one guy from another. Now they get this whole thing together. Joe Glaser, the agent, who is his agent, got as many guys as he can. Georgie

Auld, got everybody. And the most important thing is that Benny said to Joe Glaser, “Get me Ziggy Elman.” Now I came in with them to the rehearsal and Benny looks at Joe Glaser, looks around to him. He said, “I told you to get me Ziggy Elman.” He says, “That’s Ziggy.” “That’s not Ziggy Elman.” “What do you mean?” He walked away. He didn’t know Ziggy from Harry from Chris Griffin. He didn’t whose name was who. “Get me Ziggy Elman.” But when it came to playing the clarinet, that was probably some of the most greatest thrills I’ve ever had in my whole life. He can play.
